utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the registrar call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-03-69-PT, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Dermot Groome for the Office of the Prosecutor, accompanied by Mr. David Re and Ms. Skye Winner, our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. And for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Geert-Jan Knoops, lead counsel for Mr. Stanisic, and Ms. Melinda Taylor, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I am attorney-at-law Zoran Jovanovic from Belgrade, appearing on behalf of Franko Simatovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jovanovic. It was on 23rd of September, last year, that we had the last Status Conference. And since then I don't think there are many developments; however, we'll go through several issues. It is my understanding that there are no pending motions. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Not from the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: No motions pending from the Defence in the case of Mr. Stanisic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There are none. I'm very pleased to note that the pre-trial briefs are submitted in a timely manner from the Prosecution on 19th July last year with corrigendum on 22nd July. And the Defence submitted their pre-trial briefs on 18th of this month. However, I have to note and bring it to the attention of the parties that the pre-trial brief of Mr. Stanisic was filed confidentially and ex parte. Can I hear from Mr. Knoops the reason for that, the reason being why it has to be filed confidentially and in -- I think we can deal with it in open session. Not -- without going into detail, and in particular the reason for being ex parte. If you -- Mr. Knoops, you want to discuss it in private session, you can say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can just say that Your Honour is familiar with the fact that certain Rule 70 materials are disclosed to the Defence and which are now made part of the pre-trial brief. And we are under an obligation to file these materials even indirectly, when they are indirectly referred to on a confidential and ex parte basis. That is the only reason why we were obliged to file the brief confidentially ex parte. Because throughout the whole brief reference is made on several -- in several sections to Rule 70 materials. And it makes for us problematic to distinguish between non-confidential and confidential parts of the brief. Therefore, we opted to file it in its entirety as a confidential ex parte document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wonder -- yes, whether you have --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder if you have endeavoured to get the permission from the provider to disclose it to the co-accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: We did, Your Honour, but without going into further details in that respect, I would ask you to go into private session. But I can only state in public that this obligation we are under as Defence, this legal obligation, contractual obligation, also extends to the disclosure of material to the co-defendant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: At first I was concerned that in the future the Defence of Stanisic may be asking the severance of the case, but it is not the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I notice Mr. Groome was on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did see what were, I thought, two or three references to Rule 70 material. It would be the Prosecution's position that in the interest of the public nature of the proceedings that Mr. Knoops be required to file a redacted copy of his pre-trial brief that eliminates the -- or redacts the references to the Rule 70 material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. That was exactly what I was going to say. Is it possible for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: That's possible, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And that's the -- would be in the interest of the co-accused, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: I hope so. That our arguments also may benefit for the co-accused. So I have no problem confirming that with the accused, with the client. And if that is convenient we will file a redacted form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So that -- whether it be called redacted, unredacted, or public version, when do you think you can file it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Say within a week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Two weeks time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Two weeks okay, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then we shall move on to the matter -- issue of disclosure briefly. I don't think there are serious issues in relation to 66 disclosure. If you can briefly brief me on the status, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There were no outstanding issues. Mr. Knoops in his brief yesterday raised a couple of matters which I've asked Ms. Skye Winner to investigate overnight and I just have a report on those. So if it pleases the Court, I will run through those three items.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I was able to read that part as well, so if you could respond to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: One of the issues was the translations of some intercepts, the English translations of the original B/C/S intercepts. These English translations to these documents had been previously provided on the DVDs which had been provided to the Defence. When I read this query by Mr. Knoops, I did some investigation and was somewhat surprised to learn that English translations of original B/C/S documents are not always on the EDS system. They have not made the system current to include those yet. It is still a project that is being worked on. To facilitate the Defence's ability to get to those translations, however, Ms. Winner has provided another CD with a complete set of the transcripts of the intercepts in their original B/C/S, in their English translation, and has formulated a complete index which should make it quite easy for the Defence to put their hand on the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So it has been already provided to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It has been already provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It can be confirmed by the Defence right now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: You're referring to the CD-ROMs just provided?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes, they've just been provided, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. And then General Vasiljevic's interviews?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Previously the Prosecution had provided the Defence with a video of the interviews which were conducted both in English and in B/C/S. We are now in possession of an English transcript of the video and for the convenience of Defence we have provided that today. However, Ms. Winner, in checking the disclosure with respect to General Vasiljevic, has discovered that there is another interview that was conducted by a member of the Office of the Prosecution on the 8th of February, 2002, which had not been previously disclosed. An English copy of that transcript was provided today and a copy of the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond videotape will be disclosed to both accused before the end of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I hope that will resolve the matter. Any comments on that from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I can confirm that we received the CD-ROM.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same applies to me, Your Honour. I have no questions to raise in relation to this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Other matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the third query raised by Mr. Knoops in his brief had to do with the status of some translation of some documents referred to in the Prosecution pre-trial brief. These documents are now translated and have been turned over today, and they number 94 documents. I would remind the Chamber, however, that we are still outstanding 143 exhumation documents or missing person reports. They have been provided in B/C/S. For the most part these documents just contain information about the name of the victim and certain information which is easily discernible even without the translation. I would also inform the Court that we are getting most of them back, and they are in the process now of just being redacted to see if there is any witness address information or any information which should be redacted from them before they are disclosed. So I would expect by the end of February or sometime sooner all of those 143 exhumation reports will have been turned over in their English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Previously I was informed the number of reports was 154.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's why I'm an attorney and not a mathematician. It was my subtraction which was in error. But it is 143, and again we hope to have them available before the end of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What would be the situation in relation to the SDS Assembly minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: As I noted in my pre-trial remarks, they have -- translation has been requested of those. It's been requested some time ago. Because of it volume of work that CLSS is facing, it has been assigned a low priority. Many of those sessions are exhibits in pending trials now. So it is my hope that because they are needed for cases that are ongoing now, that it will be -- their priority will be elevated. But I have little control over the priority that they are being given currently in terms of being translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. If you can comment on the Defence request for hard copies of Rule 66 materials.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's just one other disclosure matter, if I might, before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If it pleases the Court, just to conclude this portion. Mr. Knoops also raised the point of footnote 291 in the Prosecution pre-trial brief which was a document he was not in possession of. That has been turned over today as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, with respect to hard copies, Your Honour, as the Court is well aware the ICTY as an institution is moving towards an electronic courtroom and electronic disclosure. All of these documents have been provided on a CD-ROM and most of them in the EDS system, but for the exception -- some exceptions. So the Prosecution is not in the position to dedicate the resources that would be required to print them out and organise them for the Defence. I would also note that a year ago we had a Status Conference on this case, and I had first proposed at that stage about the electronic disclosure and it was fully discussed, and both the Defence counsel agreed to receiving the material in electronic format then. Since that time now it has become a policy of the Tribunal to deal with these matters electronically, and so I must decline Defence's request to produce hard copies of all those materials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is the problem actually the matter who will take the burden of locating the documents and making photocopies of them?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the documents are all provided now on CD-ROMs. If the Defence want a copy of that, they can simply print out those documents and they will have them, or perhaps come to some agreement with the Registry that somebody else -- that's sent out to some outside vendor to print those documents. But the Prosecution does not maintain a hard copy of what Mr. Knoops has in electronic format. We have the exact same electronic format. So in terms of the mechanics of taking those electronic files and printing them and putting them into binders there is absolutely no savings of work. It would require us the exact same amount of time. And as Mr. Knoops pointed out in his brief yesterday, he estimates that that would be several hundreds of hours of work. That's not a resource that I have available to me at this time to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Knoops' suggestion seems to be that in the Prosecution's office there must be hard copies and making a photocopy of them they be easier than printing out them -- the documents, but it is not the case as you put it just now?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It would be tantamount to saying go down to the library and find the book and then take the book and photocopy it. If Mr. Knoops is looking for the most efficient way to make hard copies, I would suggest that the simplest and most efficient way is to simply print them from the disk. They are the exact same ones that may be scattered in files in other cases. That would be even a more enormous task, to go and pull out the discovery -- in other cases identify the particular documents that have been provided electronically and then to make photocopies of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And it is only for my information. But is search possible in that CD?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, they are searchable CDs, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They are not just scanned documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Some of them are image files, Your Honour, but they are organised by the witness to who they pertain to. So Ms. Winner has organised that CD, so each witness has their own independent folder and all the disclosure falls in under that witness. So it is not a matter of the documents being provided in any disorganised way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groom. Mr. Knoops, any observations?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, the reference the Prosecutor makes to our remark a year ago, that's of course correct. But since then the Defence is confronted with a growing amount of documents and therefore this request was made in view of the growing amount of documents. The problem for us still remains the search of certain documents on the CD-ROMs, especially for the accused where I also ask your attention to his medical situation. Perhaps we can come later to that issue. We were under the impression that most of the materials referred to in this case were identical or almost identical to the materials served in the case as mentioned in my brief in -- on page 6 under section D. And perhaps that -- if that is the case, that Defence is allowed to get copies of the materials available from the Prosecution already in a printed form. With respect to the preparation of the Defence and the trial, it simply seems to be far more efficient to have the printed version of certain documents. And indeed it -- our modest estimation is that it will indeed take several hundred hours for the Defence to print all the documents out. Yet, we have to go through all these documents with the accused. And also in the interest of his position this request is made. And I ask specifically your attention, Your Honour, to footnote 5 of our brief on page 6 belonging to section D, whereby we interpreted the current situation as embracing the obligation of the Prosecution to disclose hard copies of the -- at least the Rule 66 materials. We do agree that such an obligation does not exist or cannot be interpreted pursuant to Rule 68, but we hold the view that the Rule 66 materials should be provided to the Defence in a hard copy form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Knoops. I don't think we can go further when the Prosecution is saying that they don't have the hard copies either. They may have some materials, witness statements, and making photocopy of them may be easy. But in relation to the items they don't have in possession, there would be some difficulty. Printing out from the CD-ROM is maybe much easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Well, also considering the quite restricted -- the Defence is working under, we would like to forward the suggestion to the Honourable Trial Chamber to look for a possibility that within the Tribunal there will be a facility for printing out materials for Prosecution and Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Just a request and a suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Since this matter involves a very interesting issue, whether the obligation on the part of the Prosecution is satisfied by e-disclosure or whether they have to further provide hard copies, I think the matter is in the end for the Chamber to decide. But before that, if the parties can negotiate and make the best of it, and then, Mr. Knoops, it is for you to draw the matter to the attention of the Chamber and then the Chamber will consider the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for your consideration. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And expert report, it's done, and except for the translation of Dr. Tabeau's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It has been requested and as soon as it is available it will be disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And in his memorandum, Mr. Knoops suggested that Prosecution to draft a list of suggestions which the Defence would consider in due course. Is the Prosecution minded to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, are you referring to the suggestion with respect to 92 bis or with respect to adjudicated facts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Agreed facts and adjudicated facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I could answer the Court's question with perhaps a question to the Court. After reading the pre-trial brief of Mr. Knoops, there are facts, there are assertions in there that the Prosecution would be prepared to agree to. One of the ways we could proceed, and I want to seek the Chamber's guidance on this, if I file an application indicating which assertions that are made in that pre-trial brief that the Prosecution will not contest, will agree to, is the Chamber prepared to rule on that and make those agreed facts for the purposes of this trial?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or you can also put some questions to the Defence whether they agree or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I thought this might be more expedient since I already have what Mr. Knoops has asserted to be a fact; for example, this law existed and it meant this, that if I were to say, okay, the Prosecution agrees with that, does not contest that, that that could then become a fact that does not have to be litigated at the trial. Perhaps that would be a expedient way to at least identify some of the clearly uncontestable facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Speaking from myself, I think we need some more specific agreement by the parties. Any observation from Mr. Knoops?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I support the suggestion of the Prosecution that first step to come to a potential agreement on the 92 bis materials but also the agreed and stipulated facts could be that the Prosecution based on the pre-trial brief indeed indicates what they can agree or cannot agree. And I think I recall the session, the last Rule 65 ter conference session whereby I proposed to the legal officer of your Honourable Trial Chamber to first file a pre-trial brief and enable the Prosecution to assess the brief in view of potential agreed or disputed facts. So in line with this status -- this Rule 65 ter conference, that could be the first step to come to some mutual agreement on certain agreed and stipulated facts. I do agree, of course, with your Honourable Trial Chamber that it would probably not be the end list, but it could be a first -- first start. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: To prompt the procedure, I would be encourage the Prosecution to initiate the procedure to produce some agreed facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We will do that, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. In relation to this issue, I would like to point out that if there are facts that my colleague Mr. Groome would be disposed to agree to, facts in the pre-trial brief, then Franko Simatovic's Defence must also be informed about this, because agreed facts is something that concerns all parties. I'm not sure how we can verify this, given the fact that the motion was filed confidentially and ex parte.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That is a matter, of course. And you will be handed over the public version excluding the Rule 70 matters in due course, very soon, I would assume. I think I've done all of my agenda I've noted down. Is there any further matters for the parties to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just related to this, Mr. Knoops also raised the issue of 92 bis. I do have some observations on that if it pleases the Court now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe Mr. Knoops's position on this matter is that if the Prosecution would indicate to the Defence which particular portions of a witness's testimony it will seek to introduce via 92 bis, then the Defence will be in a position to indicate its agreement or challenge of that particular mode of taking the witness's testimony. Can I ask my learned colleague if that accurately reflects his position on that matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please. I didn't follow that part. Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you for the question, my learned colleague. Indeed it's the suggestion -- it's the suggestion from the side of the Stanisic Defence, that confronted with the potential list of Rule 92 bis materials it could be a start that the Prosecution perhaps could indicate whether the Rule 92 bis materials they intended to admit will comprise certain statements as a whole or certain statements by way of portions. We don't have, in other words, any indication as to the amount of Rule 92 bis materials as referred to in the Rule 65 ter witness list of the Prosecution. So the only thing we ask for is perhaps some more specific guidance from the side of the Prosecution as to the amount of the 92 bis materials and perhaps the portions of certain materials, or perhaps that the Prosecution thinks to file all of the materials mentioned here in its entirety at trial. And based on this guidance, the Defence is able to indicate whether or not they can admit to the Rule 92 bis materials, which the Prosecution intends to file. I hope that I clarified the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could give the Prosecution's response to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Whether it is intending -- it is minded to introduce 92 bis statement at all, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: On the 9th of July last year, the Prosecution filed a document entitled Prosecution's list of witnesses pursuant to 65 ter (E)(ii). That document contained a summary of the testimony of each of the witnesses that the Prosecution intends to call. It also included a table indicating which witnesses the Prosecution will be seeking to admit, at least part of their testimony under the Rules of 92 bis or 89(F). If you look at the summary of any of those witnesses who we have indicated it is our intention to make use of 92 bis, you will see that some of the summary is printed in italics and some is printed in standard text. Any of the text that has been printed in italics is that portion of the testimony that the Prosecution will seek to introduce via 92 bis. So if the Defence can review that document and indicate to the Prosecution which of those italics portions it is to willing to agree be taken under 92 bis, which ones it will seek to challenge, we will then be in a position then to bring appropriate submissions and applications before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, did you indicate at that -- in the document dated 9th of July whether Prosecution is going to introduce those statements without cross-examination or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have a copy of the table - if it helps the Court, and I believe -- I think one is being handed up to you now - for each witness the Prosecution has indicated whether it is our intention to take the evidence viva voce, completely 92 bis, or partially 92 bis'd. For those witnesses that we've indicated will be partially 92 bis'd or entirely 92 bis'd, if you look at their summary later in the document you will see that the paragraphs that are italicised are those paragraphs which the Prosecution submits would be appropriately taken under 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Will that answer be sufficient to Mr. Knoops?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That clarifies the position of the Prosecution and enables the Defence to respond. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any other matters? Is there any other matters for the parties to raise? Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in relation to disclosure, I have nothing further to say. However, the Defence has informed the OTP, given the fact that we did not hold a 65 ter meeting, about an issue that we wish to raise. The same has been done by my colleague, Mr. Knoops. We have a list of 24 persons submitted to the Defence team by the Republic of Serbia, Ministry of Justice. These persons are persons that the indicted must not get in touch with during the --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm not able to hear the translation anymore. I don't know if anyone else is experiencing the same problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm hearing. But you have to turn up the volume. If Mr. Jovanovic says some words in order for Mr. Groome and others to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. Of course. I will repeat. The issue that the Defence wishes to raise at this time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you following, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, of course, Your Honour. The Defence wishes to raise the following question. It's about a list containing the names of 24 persons submitted to the Defence by the Ministry of Justice of the Republic of Serbia. The list actually contains the names of persons that the accused must not contact during their provisional release. The list was submitted at the request of the Defence. The Defence has managed to find out that such a list is in existence and that it was submitted to members of the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Serbia at a meeting with representatives of the ICTY in Belgrade. This list was forwarded to the Defence 25 days after it was given to the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Serbia. It contains, as I said, 24 names. Only a few of the names are the same as those mentioned on the 65 ter list of the OTP. The remaining persons were not indicated as potential witnesses pursuant to 65 ter. In relation to some of these persons, there is no indication whatsoever of these persons in the OTP's pre-trial brief. Therefore, this begs the question: What is the status of these persons? And why exactly is the OTP trying to prevent the accused from contacting these persons in that case. What the Defence wants to know is whether the OTP has any particular status in mind for these persons and what the role of these persons will be in the course of further proceedings. I will confine myself to citing two examples in relation to problems that may or may not arise from these actions. No motion was addressed to the Chamber that the Defence would then respond to. It was forwarded directly to the police by the ICTY office in Belgrade, and immediately after the Defence team found out that such a list was in existence we filed a request for the list to be forwarded to us, noting also that we would be raising this issue at a Status Conference before the ICTY. In relation to one person, the name was stated incorrectly; therefore, the Defence can only assume who this person is. In relation to a different person, his function or official position is cited as financier. This is something that is not indicated in the pre-trial brief. This person is a close relation of one of the accused, and for 25 days he had not been informed that he was not supposed to contact this person. Fortunately, this person currently resides abroad, so therefore no contact was ever established. So what the Defence wishes to have is an update on the exact status of these persons, and if any changes have been made to their status, we would want to know whether they would have any role in these proceedings. What follows is that statements by these persons should be discussed. If indeed these persons do not have the status of witnesses in this case, the question remains why there must be no contact between the accused and these persons. In relation to another issue that was raised in this letter in relation to the fear that exists for the personal safety of the accused Franko Simatovic, the Defence contacted the OTP before this Status Conference, and we have obtained all the information that we deemed necessary. Therefore, we no longer have a need to swell on this particular issue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jovanovic. Yes, Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was indeed also about to raise this matter, but I was under the impression that you first wanted to deal with the whole agenda for today. But as you may have noted, the Defence in the case of Mr. Simatovic did address the same issue in our brief of yesterday under section A, in which section we also elaborated on the potential ramifications of this so-called order. And we also delineated our view that this so-called order is violating the rules of your Tribunal. And also we indicate that we feel seriously endangered by this action which also is potentially undermining the proper Defence preparation. And therefore we proposed in the Defence of Mr. Stanisic for the prompt intervention of the Honourable Trial Chamber or, alternatively, we are ready file and are able to file a motion to this extent because we think this relates to a very principal matter which goes at the heart of the Defence preparation. And therefore you find on pages 1 until 3 of our brief several suggestions to that extent. And our brief in section A closes with the readiness of the Defence to file an official motion to that extent which could enable your Honourable Trial Chamber to rule on this rather fundamental issue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: To clarify, it is different from the regime of protection of a witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And speaking for myself, I have never heard of this kind of list or order. And, Mr. Knoops, you suggested there for reasons of judicial economy you suggest the Chamber to resolve the matter without filing a written motion. But given the significance of the matter, I would rather encourage the parties to put it in a written filing in order for the Chamber to consider the matter. But before that, if you have anything to say, Mr. Groome on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was brought to my attention in Mr. Knoops's briefing yesterday when I was provided also a copy of the letter and Mr. Jovanovic earlier today provided me with a copy of the letter he received. I have found out some details, but if it is the Court's wish to take this important matter in writing, it probably is better for me to further investigate what exactly occurred and to put it in a written submission to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But if you could tell us what it is about briefly and orally now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, what I have been able to discover, Your Honour, is that after the Appeals Chamber affirmed this Trial Chamber's provisional release of the two accused in Belgrade, the field office of the ICTY was contacted by members of the Serbian/Montenegrin government, and they formally requested that that representative of the Tribunal provide them with the names of all the witnesses, including the protected witnesses, in this case. That person forwarded that request to the investigator responsible for the case. That investigator thought it was inappropriate to, in that manner, disclose the names of protected witnesses and declined to do so, but did offer a list of names of people that he thought there might be some concern if there was contact between the accused and these people. And that information was then in turn provided to the government officials that requested it. The OTP did not initiate this correspondence. It was a request by the government. And OTP has made no request whatsoever to the government with respect to restricting any additional restrictions on the accused outside of what the Court has ordered. What I might contribute to this discussion is in fairness to the government is that aside from their undertakings to the Chamber, they also have a legitimate police function to perform and to protect their citizens. When these two gentlemen were provisionally released, there was some reaction in Belgrade; in fact, one of the most prominent human rights activists publicly stated that she had information that these two men had engaged in the intimidation of witnesses. It's not for -- I would urge the Court to get more information from the government of Serbia, I think that in the event that they may be more involved here. Again, they may be exercising legitimate lawful restrictions completely aside from what -- and not simply just simply interpreting the Chamber's order. From the Prosecution's view, we have no role to play in the regulation of the terms of their provisional release. The Court has issued a clear order on that. If the government of Serbia and Montenegro were hoping that the Prosecution would clarify your order, well, that is a misdirected request. We have no role to play in that and believe that it's a matter between the Chamber, the Defence, and the governmental authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. I would prefer the matter to be taken more seriously and prudently by way of written filing, unless the parties wish to raise urgently at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are ready to file a motion already next week to this extent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber will consider the matter. Any other matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: After you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: The final matter is probably not for a public session to elaborate on but just to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I've noted the -- some confidential matters you've raised in your brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question is whether you have to raise it in a Status Conference or is it enough for you to file a written filing drawing the attention of the Chamber to what you've written down in your brief?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The letter is indeed the case. This is for just by way of information of the Honourable Trial Chamber and the Prosecution about the status quo on the specific topic. I refer to section D of my brief. I will not rephrase it in public. If the Trial Chamber appreciates, and the Prosecution, we can file the whole report we referred to in section B of our brief in its entirety with a motion to the extent as suggested in our brief. But we thought it is appropriate to raise the matter -- at least bring the matter to the attention of Your Honour in a view of the topic which was also on the agenda on the anticipated length of the trial, et cetera. So we are happy to leave it as it is, bring it to your attention, and we can deal with the topic in a written filing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that any request to change the conditions of provisional release be done in writing so we can have a full opportunity to respond carefully to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Prosecution didn't respond to the earlier motion from the Defence in relation to the variance -- variation of the status in relation to the provisional release?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we took no opposition to that, but this seems to be somewhat different. If Mr. Knoops is seeking an oral variation of that order, the Prosecution would like to know more details about where it is proposed that the accused is permitted to go and for what period of time and perhaps some further assurances from the government that they will be able to fulfill their obligations to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry. I'd like to be clear about this. You're referring to his visit to his mother's grave?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. What I'm referring to at this point is what Mr. Knoops has referred to just recently and is in his brief about the accused being allowed to leave Belgrade for additional medical care. It is that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. It will be put into writing?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we will put it into writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the Prosecution will be able to respond to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have one additional matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It has recently come to my attention that the Stanisic Defence has made contact with a former member -- a former senior member of the Office of the Prosecutor and solicited confidential information about events surrounding the surrender of another accused. I'm not sure to what end this was done, but I must insist if there is information that the Stanisic Defence believes is important, relevant, and is in possession of the Office of the Prosecutor or has to do with former employees acting in their official capacity, that he make an official request, rather than soliciting it from employees who are still bound by a duty of confidentiality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Defence must have heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Your Honour. But it was in no way meant to circumvent any rule, and we were already notified by the particular person to make an official filing to that extent. So we will ask the Prosecution officially to perhaps cooperate on this issue, which is already referred to in the pre-trial brief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are there any other matters for the Defence to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Final matter will be the next Status Conference. I was informed that that would be 20th of May, 2005. I would like to have it on Thursday, 19th of May, at 3.00. If there -- should there be a change, I'll let the parties know. The hearing now -- is now adjourned.
